1-15231-2-1.subevent: A mortar attack occurred in northern Faryab province on Thursday morning.
At least four civilians were killed and 10 others were wounded in the attack.
The incident happened around 11:00am local time after a mortar round landed in a market in Shareen Tagab district.
Abdul Karim Yourish, a spokesman for the provincial police chief, said the mortar was fired 'by the Taliban' to target security forces.
Yourish added that all the victims were civilians who were at the market to shop.
The Taliban has not commented on the attack.

0-4495-1-1.subevent: Tunisia Youth Impact uses cooking contests to encourage rural women to vote in the presidential election.
On October 12, a Voticook cooking contest is held in the rural town of Echamine.
The national turnout in the first round of the election was 48.98%.
Wafa Tarhouni explains that the contest is a practice vote where women compete through their dishes.
Volunteers mimic real voting conditions, replacing ink with a water and shampoo mixture.
The contest is held at the home of Hinda Jlass, who is participating.
Hinda Jlass says the event is about getting together and plans to vote in the election for the second time.
Seven competitors present their dishes to about fifty electors.
Electors taste the dishes and vote using the same procedure as the real election.
ISIE members and EU observer Stefan Ziegler are present; Ziegler says it is good for Tunisian democracy.
After voting, ballots are counted and volunteers point out potential mistakes.
Najwa Jlass wins the contest and says she will vote in the real election.

6-18979-2-t.subevent: Crime adapts to societal changes, evolving from individual violations to organized crime.
The Sicilian Cosa Nostra adapted to a changing economy from village-agrarian to urban-industrial.
Organized crime has become networks and alliances across national boundaries.
Drug trafficking leads to corruption, threats, and killings of law enforcement and judges.
Drug proceeds are laundered and reinvested into the legal economy.
Organized crime seeks a power monopoly using any means for profit without concern for others.
Common criminality and organized crime intersect, with many organized criminals starting as thieves.
Organized crime develops a mythology of invincibility used to intimidate.
Informants' confessions have helped document organized crime.
Nigerian criminal enterprises emerged from economic downturn and are highly successful due to bribery of officials.
Nigerian criminal groups are flexible with three types of structures: pyramidal hierarchy, flexible networks, and independent cells.
Nigerian groups target the US and Britain, engaging in heroin trafficking and scams, including a 1999 advance fee fraud and a 1997 check theft, with proceeds funding narcotics smuggling.

13-wiki-img/24416-1/24416-1-1.subevent: The State Emergency Commission held a meeting.
The commission decided to suspend all movements of automobiles, buses, and railway, but air transport, between Ulaanbaatar and 21 aimags from 08.00 am of February 23 to 08.00 am of February 27.

0-4931-1-4.subevent: Sheriff Turnbull said the tragedy happened because Captain David Traill ignored five fuel warnings.
He called the decision 'conscious' with 'fatal consequences' for 10 people.
The police helicopter crashed into the Clutha bar at 22:22 on 29 November 2013.
The crash killed 10 people and injured 31 others.
Mark O'Prey's father expressed anger, saying Captain Traill was made a 'fall guy'.
Clutha owner Alan Crossan expressed 'shock and disappointment' at the report.
Sheriff Turnbull heard testimony from families, experts, and eyewitnesses during the inquiry.
The crash occurred because the helicopter's engines 'flamed out' due to fuel exhaustion.
The fuel tanks were depleted because Captain Traill failed to ensure at least one fuel transfer pump switch was on.
Sheriff Turnbull said the central question was why the pilot ignored the low fuel warnings.
The accident would not have happened if the pilot had followed the normal procedure for low fuel warnings.
The pilot's checklist required landing within 10 minutes of a fuel warning.
Sheriff Turnbull described the failure as 'inexplicable'.
He said Captain Traill 'took a chance' that the warnings were erroneous.
Sheriff Turnbull said the helicopter should have had a warning when both fuel transfer pumps were off.
Both pumps were switched off during the flight.
Sheriff Turnbull said the circumstances were so unusual they are unlikely to be repeated.
He praised the dignity of those who attended the inquiry.
Sheriff Turnbull criticized the delay in confirming no criminal proceedings and in lodging the inquiry.
He said the Crown Office's Helicopter Incidents Investigation Team was under-resourced.
He noted that a FAI into the Sumburgh crash was still pending.
A Crown Office spokesperson acknowledged the time taken was longer than desirable and promised improvements.
Airbus Helicopters expressed sadness and said they noted the findings.

3-17441-15-t.subevent: Economy Minister Roberto Gualtieri said that Confindustria's forecast of a 6% fall in gross domestic product this year due to the coronavirus crisis is realistic.
On Tuesday, national business association Confindustria said the outbreak would cause a serious recession in 2020.
Gualtieri told Il Fatto Quotidiano that the estimates are realistic and the Italian economy can aim for a vigorous rebound.
The government is not due to give its own estimates of the impact until the end of April when it publishes the Document of Economy and Finance.
Italy's output rose 0.3% last year, and the government expected it to grow 0.6% this year before the coronavirus emerged at the end of February.
At the end of March, two sources told Reuters that the Treasury expected the economy to contract around 3% this year.
Gualtieri said a new stimulus package, set to be approved this month, will be significantly larger than the 25 billion euros passed in March and sufficient for the entire epidemic.
He said it will include an extension of state-backed guarantees for companies seeking liquidity, unemployment benefits, and support for people on low incomes.
Gualtieri said using the European Stability Mechanism under current conditions is not an option and that Europe needs a coordinated shared fiscal policy.
He said new solutions are needed to grant parity of conditions and define an adequate shared and responsible response.

21-31050-3-1.subevent: Yoshiro Mori resigned as president of the Tokyo Olympic Committee after making sexist remarks about women.
Mori announced his resignation at a meeting of the Olympic Committee's executive board and council.
Mori had reportedly said women talk too much and have a strong sense of rivalry during a board meeting.
After criticism, Mori apologized and retracted his remarks, acknowledging they were inappropriate.
Mori apologized again while announcing his resignation, saying his comments caused big trouble.
Mori stated that his comments were misinterpreted and that he was not prejudiced against women.
IOC President Thomas Bach said the IOC respects Mori's decision and will work with his successor.
Japan extended its state of emergency in Tokyo and other regions by another month due to COVID-19.
Japan reported its worst one-day death toll for COVID-19 with 121 new deaths and has not started mass vaccinations.
Nearly 80% of the Japanese public said the Olympics should be canceled or further delayed.
Hundreds of Olympic volunteers quit and local organizers received thousands of complaints after Mori's remarks.
Tennis player Naomi Osaka called Mori's comments 'really ignorant' and swimmer Kosuke Hagino called them 'very unfortunate.'
Several sponsors voiced concerns over Mori's remarks.
Female opposition lawmakers wore white with roses in protest of Mori's remarks.
Japan ranked 121st out of 153 countries in the World Economic Forum's 2020 gender gap index.

33-2542-7-1.subevent: Marines used the Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) on USS Boxer to down a hostile Iranian drone.
The drone was downed 1,000 yards from the ship during a transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
MADIS is a combination of electronic jammers, radars, and gun systems mounted on an MRZR on the bow, powered by a gasoline generator.
Naval analyst Thomas Callender said the encounter is the first known kill by a new generation of electronic warfare and directed energy weapons.
The Navy and Marines are concerned about swarms of cheap but lethal unmanned vehicles overwhelming defenses.
Firing expensive missiles to intercept a cheap drone puts Americans at a cost disadvantage.
Boxer fields RIM-7 Sea Sparrow missiles costing about $170,000 each and RIM-116 Rolling Airframe Missiles costing nearly a million dollars apiece.
The Navy has tested less expensive options like 5-inch deck guns and the Phalanx Close-in Weapons System with limited success.
Callender said those options still cost thousands of dollars in rounds, while MADIS puts the cost exchange ratio in favor of the U.S.
In 2014, the Navy deployed a 30-kilowatt laser aboard a ship that cost about a dollar per shot.
The Navy plans to install a 60-kilowatt HELIOS directed energy weapon on a destroyer in 2021.
The Navy is also developing the Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program (SEWIP) Block III for non-kinetic disabling of enemy missiles and UAVs.
Callender said using systems like MADIS is less escalatory and provides deniability.

1-15230-2-1.subevent: In Bamyan province, children help with the potato harvest; many girls attend school for the first time, including 10-year-old Hamida who says she never went until last year.

Unicef reports that 3.2 million girls are now educated, a dramatic rise since the Taliban ban ended in 2001, but the female literacy rate has only tripled to 13% and women still face inequality and child marriages.

Gulnaz was raped, charged with adultery, gave birth in jail, and was later pardoned by President Karzai after international outcry; women's groups have criticized Karzai for not taking a stronger stand on women's rights.
At Suriya school in Kabul, girls practice cricket with a male coach, supported by Afghan Connection and Marylebone Cricket Club; one 12-year-old girl says she wants to be a journalist.

Outside big cities, changes are patchy; 60% of the 4.2 million out-of-school children are girls, most in rural areas and conflict zones where conservative attitudes and Taliban activity limit education.
Teaching in southern Afghanistan is dangerous.
There is anxiety that momentum for girls' education may not survive the US withdrawal in 2014, but Education Minister Farooq Wardak insists it will last.
At a school opening in Bamyan, Wardak says only when women feel they own the nation can Afghanistan succeed.
Afghan Connection has funded over 30 schools, focusing on rural areas; director Dr. Sarah Fayne says the key is winning acceptance through proximity and female teachers.
Dr. Fayne says she believes the changes of the past decade are permanent.
Hamida works in the fields and helps at home but walks 2km to school six days a week.
Hamida's mother, who is 30 years old, says there was no school in her time, and Hamida wants to be a doctor.

6-19726-1-1.subevent: Biomerieux gave its proprietary formula to the Canadian government for free.
In March, Canada passed emergency legislation giving the government and third parties the right to produce patented goods without consent.
Canada did not force Biomerieux to agree, but the option was available.
Biomerieux did not respond to questions about similar arrangements with other governments or the revenue impact.
Biomerieux reported a 21.5% increase in first-quarter sales due in part to demand for reagent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada described the arrangement as a temporary license at no cost.
PHAC said its manufacturing was in development and testing, aiming to alleviate shortages soon.
Biomerieux's Canadian unit emailed customers in early April saying the move clears testing backlogs and it is boosting own production.
The chemicals in short supply are reagents used to extract RNA from patient samples.
Biomerieux extraction equipment is widely used in Canada, primarily in Ontario, contributing to a testing slowdown in late March.
PHAC said the deal is an interim solution because its facilities are not for long-term manufacturing.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing.

9-21075-1-t.subevent: The Portuguese government announced a new lockdown and released the final list of activities that must close as of 0h on Friday.
The final list contains a few changes from the version discussed in the Council of Ministers.
Driving schools are allowed to remain open only for conducting tests and exams.
Tutoring centers and language schools were removed from the final list, meaning they must close.
Leisure time activities must also close.
Recreational activities including nightclubs, circuses, amusement parks, water parks, and similar venues must close.
Cultural activities such as auditoriums, cinemas, theaters, museums, libraries, and exhibition venues must close, except for election campaign events.
Educational activities including tutoring centers, language schools, and driving schools (except exams) must close.
Sports activities in closed venues, including fields, pavilions, pools, gyms, and stadiums, must close.
Activities in open spaces and public roads such as cycling tracks, nautical shows, and folk festivals must close.
Gambling establishments including casinos, bingo halls, and similar venues must close.
Restaurants and similar establishments must close except for delivery and takeaway.
Spas and similar establishments must close.
A list of essential services remains open, including supermarkets, pharmacies, health services, banks, and hotels.
Hotels, tourist accommodations, and local lodging establishments remain open.
The article corrects an earlier statement that tutoring centers would remain open.

1-14903-2-2.subevent: Looting, arson, attacks on police stations and vehicles, destruction of an ambulance, and daily protests ending in clashes with security forces have occurred in Chile.
President Sebastian Pinera sent an urgent bill to Congress requesting the army be allowed to safeguard key installations without declaring a state of emergency.
The government stated that about one-third of the estimated $1.5bn destruction was caused by criminal gangs, common criminals, drug traffickers and anarchists.
Graffiti messages such as 'Accumulate fury' and 'make the cuicos (the rich) shiver' were seen in Santiago.
A protester named Mario said that peaceful demonstrations have achieved nothing.
Mario lost his job as an assistant accountant.
Maria said that they need to shake the elite out of their comfort zone and make them feel fear to force action.
Maria said that the rich and powerful threw the first stone by discriminating and leaving them without education and healthcare.
Maria Olga said that those causing destruction cannot be Chileans and she does not recognize the country.
Mario said they are not asking for jewels or gold, only basic things like a decent income and basic services.
Maria expressed anger at the injustice she sees, such as her mother being unable to get hospital treatment for her grandparents and the huge differences in standard of living.
A new study showed that 58 percent of Chileans belong to the lower-middle-class or 'vulnerable class' who cannot access their basic needs under the current system.
Mario said he does not believe in voting and does not feel represented by any political party.

0-4407-1-1.subevent: A double-decker bus overturned into a field in Devon on Saturday 5 October.
Emergency services declared a major incident after the crash on the A385 between Totnes and Paignton at around 11am.
A multi-agency approach was adopted by emergency services, deploying a large number of police, fire, and ambulance vehicles.
Numerous air ambulances attended the scene.
At 5:30pm, Devon and Cornwall Police released a statement.
The statement said that 37 people sustained injuries, with eight described as having potentially serious injuries.
Police confirmed that the road will close again from 7am on Sunday 6 October while emergency crews recover the bus.
Police added that there is significant pressure on local health services and urged people not to attend A&E unless it is a real emergency.

1-14955-1-t.subevent: President Trump pointed to a bar chart showing one country's coronavirus death toll per capita stretched out beyond all others, which was Belgium.
The graph placed the U.S. rate below six European nations.
Belgian minister Denis Ducarme called Trump's display 'macabre' and 'level zero' politics.
Ducarme tweeted that Belgium's method of counting COVID-19 deaths is the most exhaustive possible.
Belgium includes deaths suspected of being virus-related, whether the victim was tested or not.
As of Wednesday, Belgium counted 6,262 deaths from COVID-19, roughly 540 per million citizens.
More than half of those deaths were in nursing homes; of those, only 4.5% were confirmed infected, yet all are counted in the national tally.
Belgian authorities faced pressure to change their counting method due to negative perception.
Prime Minister Sophie Wilmès suggested the count has been exaggerated.
Emmanuel André, spokesman for the government's coronavirus task force, defended the method and said other countries are copying the Belgian surveillance model.
André said, 'When you don't know, it's more difficult to act.'
Experts at Wednesday's briefing said the country likely hit the coronavirus' peak on April 12.
On Friday, a special task force is due to unveil a gradual exit strategy from lockdown measures.

7-36661-5-2.subevent: The Technical University of Denmark shut down, but Professor Anders Wolff continues working on the CoronaDX project to develop three new measuring instruments for fast on-site coronavirus diagnosis.
Project partner Anders Fomsgaard from Statens Seruminstitut also continues working because two instruments are scheduled for emergency use in October and the third in March 2021.
Several research teams are working on a vaccine, but approval is 1-2 years away, so it is essential to develop technology to quickly separate healthy from infected people.

The fastest instrument will give diagnosis in less than one minute, the slowest in less than an hour, and all three are designed to be very easy to use, like a pregnancy test, for use in clinics or at home.
On-site testing saves time and resources, decreases pressure on central laboratories, and reduces risk of hospital staff infection by enabling immediate quarantine.
Quarantine-affected persons can get immediate diagnosis and resume normal lives if not infected, keeping more people working during an epidemic.
Professor Fomsgaard, responsible for two instruments including the fastest, says the speed and ease could increase healthcare system effectiveness and become a new tool for diagnosing viral diseases.
Professors Wolff and Fomsgaard expect to have emergency use permit in Denmark by October for the possible second wave of coronavirus.
Under normal conditions development would take years, but Wolff says the research community is collaborating across countries rather than competing, enabling fast progress.
The three instruments use three different measurement methods and the technology is the newest in the field, recently developed in an EU project for poultry diseases.
Wolff says the measuring instrument is ready but new reagents are needed to react with the virus; emergency regulations allow field testing earlier than usual.
As early as June, two Chinese partners will test two of the instruments in the field in China.

2-35026-1-t.subevent: France seizes British scallop dredger Cornelis Gert Jan and escorts it to Le Havre.
A second British vessel is given a verbal warning by French authorities.
French minister Annick Girardin announces the seizure and says 'It's not war, but it is a fight.'
France lists potential sanctions against Britain, including extra customs checks from Nov. 2 and a threat to cut electricity exports.
The British government calls the French reaction 'disappointing and disproportionate.'
Environment minister George Eustice challenges France's claim that the boat lacked a license and says the threatened steps may violate international law.
Eustice warns that Britain will respond with an 'appropriate and calibrated response' if the steps are carried out.
French European Affairs Minister Clement Beaune says 'we need to speak the language of strength' because Britain has refused to grant enough licenses.
Girardin clarifies that France cannot cut electricity to Britain but can raise tariffs.
The European Commission says it will continue talks with Britain and France.
The skipper of the seized boat is under investigation for illegal scallop dredging, while the boat's owners say it had a valid license.

Barrie Deas says France appears determined to escalate the row before the presidential election, and Bruno Margolle reports that 15 license requests have moved to 'under consideration' since the boat was held.

0-4882-1-2.subevent: The X-37B Orbital Test Vehicle Mission 5 landed at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility on Oct. 27, 2019, at 3:51 a.m.
The spaceplane conducted on-orbit experiments for 780 days during its mission, breaking its own record by being in orbit for more than two years.
The total number of days spent on-orbit for the entire X-37B program reached 2,865 days.
Secretary of the Air Force Barbara Barrett stated that the X-37B continues to demonstrate the importance of a reusable spaceplane.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David L. Goldfein stated that the safe return after breaking its endurance record results from innovative government-industry partnership, and that the sky is no longer the limit for the Air Force.

Randy Walden, Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office director, stated that the X-37B completed its longest flight to date and successfully completed all mission objectives, including hosting Air Force Research Laboratory experiments and providing a ride for small satellites.
Lt. Col. Jonathan Keen, X-37B program manager, stated that the milestone demonstrates commitment to conducting experiments for America's future space exploration.
This was the second time the X-37B landed at the Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility, following Mission 4 which landed after 718 days in orbit.
Brig. Gen. Doug Schiess, 45th Space Wing commander, stated that the team's hard work and dedication culminated in the safe and successful landing of the X-37B.
The fifth mission launched on Sept. 7, 2017, from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida, on-board a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster.
The Air Force is preparing to launch the sixth X-37B mission from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in 2020.

9-21348-5-1.subevent: Many Central American families arriving at the U.S. border flee armed violence, including killings, gang recruitment, rape, harassment, and death threats.
Historically, Central Americans migrated for economic reasons after the internal armed conflicts of the 1970s and 1980s.
Today's migrant flow includes more families, newborns, children, and pregnant women escaping life-or-death situations rather than just male heads of household.
The 1996 U.S. Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act led to deportations of convicted criminals to Central America, which expanded gangs like MS-13 and Barrio 18.
The region's civil wars, inequality, mass incarceration, and weak institutions created a gang problem that has taken over both rural and urban areas.
Parents in gang-plagued 'red zones' spend money on private transport and after-school programs to keep their children away from gangs.
In El Salvador, boys as young as 12 are targeted for gang recruitment, and girls are targeted for sexual abuse or forced membership.
Gang recruitment is gradual, starting with gifts and invitations, and families refusing to leave are threatened.
Despite prevention efforts, gangs remain defiant and have penetrated the social fabric, making police operations alone insufficient.
Governments rely on security crackdowns, which indirectly cause locals to flee due to fear of police and gang confrontations.
Residents are caught in daily armed confrontations between gangs and security forces, and teenagers are harassed by police.
Many Central American families feel stuck between the dangerous trip north and life-threatening conditions at home, so they choose to migrate despite U.S. policies.

0-4546-1-2.subevent: Three people died in Southern California wildfires.
Evacuation orders were lifted in Los Angeles County and parts of Riverside County.
The Saddleridge Fire ignited late Thursday in Sylmar, destroying over 30 structures and burning over 7,900 acres.
Officials issued emergency declarations and secured a FEMA grant for the fire.
At least 31 structures were damaged, with 13 destroyed, and over 1,000 firefighters responded.
Strong Santa Ana winds and dry conditions fueled the fire, forcing freeway closures and evacuations.
The National Weather Service warned of Red Flag conditions despite weaker winds.
276 minors were evacuated from a juvenile detention center, and a hospital was placed under shelter-in-place.
One civilian died from cardiac arrest and a firefighter sustained a minor injury.
The cause of the fire is unknown; it was first reported at 9 p.m. Thursday.
PG&E proactively shut off power to 800,000 customers in Northern and Central California.
The Sandalwood Fire in Riverside County was 68% contained at 1,000 acres, with two deaths and 74 structures destroyed.
Southern California Edison cut power to over 21,000 customers, later reduced to 54.
SoCalGas reported no indications of damage or leaks at the Aliso Canyon facility.

1-15178-2-1.subevent: The Portuguese Episcopal Conference announced on Jan. 21 that public Masses would be suspended from Jan. 23 due to the extreme gravity of the coronavirus crisis.
The bishops stated that it is a moral imperative for all citizens to take maximum sanitary precautions to avoid contagion.
Portugal experienced a surge in COVID-19 deaths, with 609,000 cases and 9,920 deaths recorded as of Jan. 22.
This was the second suspension of public worship by the bishops, the first being in March 2020 with restrictions eased at the end of May.
The bishops said that public Masses, catechesis, and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings would be suspended, and they called on priests to offer livestreamed Masses.
Earlier in January, the bishops called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
They said funerals could be celebrated according to norms issued in May 2020 requiring social distancing.
A Lenten retreat for the bishops scheduled for Feb. 22-26 was canceled.
The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima announced it would broadcast three Masses and two rosary prayers daily via its website during the suspension.
Shrine rector Fr. Carlos Cabecinhas commented that following via television is not the same as being physically present but is the only possible way to participate now.

1-14989-2-3.subevent: A new study shows that the megatooth shark Otodus megalodon was the largest shark to ever swim in our planet’s oceans.
O. megalodon lived approximately 23 to 3.6 million years ago and is extinct.
The exact cause of its extinction is debated, likely a combination of environmental change and competition.
Little is known about its life-appearance because sharks have cartilaginous skeletons that decay, leaving only teeth.
A recent study concluded that a full-grown megalodon could reach about 50 feet in length.
A new study published in Historical Biology shows how unique the size of this species was.
Kenshu Shimada compiled a database of 70 shark species and used functions from present-day sharks to infer size from fossil teeth.
The study found that non-planktivorous sharks have a general size limit of 23 feet, while plankton-eating sharks can reach 26-32 feet.
Sharks got on average bigger in the last 65 million years, but O. megalodon at 46-50 feet was exceptionally large.
Warm-bloodedness and oophagy have been proposed as adaptations for gigantism, with warm-bloodedness documented in great white sharks and oophagy likely evolving repeatedly.
Based on growth models, a newborn megalodon was already 9 feet long.

10-6887-1-2.subevent: Dozens of climate activists invaded U.S. asset manager BlackRock's office in central Paris.
The activists called for the fund to pull out of fossil fuel investments.
Green activists from Extinction Rebellion and Fridays for Future entered the building and reached the fourth floor.
Emilia, a 15-year-old Fridays for Future member, said they want to change the capitalistic system.
Activists wrote tags such as 'I want to live' or 'Murderers' on the walls.
They blocked the entrance with ropes and rolling office cabinets.
BlackRock condemned the violent intrusion and vandalism in a statement.
BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned company boards in January to step up efforts to tackle climate change.
Fink said his firm would exit investments that presented high sustainability-related risk, including thermal coal producers.

Extinction Rebellion last month targeted energy group Royal Dutch Shell's headquarters in The Hague and McKinsey & Co's London office, and staged a demonstration at a Brussels car show at which 185 protesters were detained.

11-23153-1-1.subevent: Zanzibar’s first Vice President and ACT Wazalendo’s Chairman Maalim Seif Sharif Hamad has died at the age of 77.
He was admitted to Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar es Salaam on February 9, 2021.
He died on Wednesday, February 17, 2021 at 11:26 in the morning.
The cause of death was not made clear, but on January 31 he was reportedly hospitalized at Mnazi Mmoja Hospital in Zanzibar after allegedly testing positive for Coronavirus.
President of Zanzibar and Chairman of the Revolutionary Council Hussein Mwinyi announced his death on February 17, declaring seven days of national mourning.
President Magufuli sent condolences to Zanzibar’s President and the people of Zanzibar on the death of the ACT Chairman.
President Magufuli wrote a condolence message on his Twitter handle.

1-15800-4-1.subevent: At 11 p.m. EDT on July 5, Tropical Depression 5 strengthened into Tropical Storm Edouard.
On July 6 at 1:45 a.m. EDT, the MODIS instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite analyzed Tropical Storm Edouard’s cloud tops in infrared light.
MODIS found a small area of powerful thunderstorms northeast of the center of circulation with cloud top temperatures as cold as minus 70 degrees Fahrenheit.
Southwesterly wind shear was pushing the strongest storms northeast of the tropical cyclone’s center.
Satellite imagery indicated that the rest of Edouard was comprised of an exposed swirl of low- to mid-level clouds.
Winds from the west were displacing the bulk of clouds and showers from Edouard and pushing them to the east.
At 5 a.m. EDT on July 6, the center of Tropical Storm Edouard was located near latitude 39.0 degrees north and longitude 53.6 degrees west.
Maximum sustained winds were near 40 mph with higher gusts, and the estimated minimum central pressure was 1008 millibars.
Little significant change in strength is forecast before Edouard becomes post-tropical later in the day.
Edouard was moving toward the northeast near 36 mph and this motion is expected to continue for the next couple of days as it tracks toward the United Kingdom.

National Hurricane Center forecaster Jack Beven noted that the cyclone is in a region of strong southwesterly vertical wind shear, heading for colder water, and approaching a frontal system, which should lead to extratropical transition between 12 to 24 hours, with possible slight strengthening, after which the extratropical low should persist for another 24 hours before dissipation.

0-4813-2.subevent: A report found that a series of failures led to the crash of a Lion Air flight, killing 189 people and leading to the grounding of the Boeing 737 Max.
Investigators said faults by Boeing, Lion Air, and pilots caused the crash.
Five months after the Lion Air crash, an Ethiopian Airlines plane crashed, killing all 157 people on board, which led to the grounding of the entire 737 Max fleet.
On Friday, Indonesian air crash investigators released their final report detailing the events that caused the Lion Air jet to plunge into the Java Sea.
The report found that the jet should have been grounded before the fatal flight due to an earlier cockpit issue, but because the issue was not recorded properly, the plane was allowed to take off.
The report found that a crucial sensor bought from a repair shop in Florida had not been properly tested, and the US aviation regulator revoked that company's certification.

The sensor fed information to the MCAS system, which repeatedly pushed the plane's nose down, and investigators identified issues with the system, including incorrect assumptions about its behavior and deficiencies in training.

The report found that the first officer, who had performed poorly in training, struggled to run through procedures and was flying the plane just before the fatal dive, and the captain had not briefed him properly when handing over controls.
The report found that 31 pages were missing from the plane's maintenance log.
Indonesian authorities laid out recommendations for Boeing, including that it redesign MCAS and provide adequate information in pilot manuals and training.
Boeing said it was addressing the recommendations and taking actions to enhance the safety of the 737 Max.
Boeing ousted Kevin McAllister, chief executive of Boeing Commercial Airplanes.
Boeing said it expected the 737 Max to be re-certified for flying by the end of the year.
A Lion Air spokesman said the crash was an unthinkable tragedy and that corrective actions were essential.
Revelations emerged that in 2016, Boeing employees exchanged messages about issues with MCAS while the plane was being certified.
In documents provided to lawmakers, a pilot wrote that he had run into unexpected trouble during tests and had basically lied to regulators unknowingly.
Boeing developed a training update and expected regulators to allow the planes to return to the skies before the beginning of 2020.
Boeing's profits more than halved to $895m in the third quarter, and the firm said it would cut production of its 787 Dreamliner, blaming trade uncertainties.
Boeing boss Dennis Muilenburg was stripped of his title as chairman by the board but remains as chief executive.

1-16084-3-1.subevent: International aid organizations, human rights groups, and doctors sounded alarms about the potential for a coronavirus catastrophe in overcrowded Greek refugee camps.
An outbreak of COVID-19 occurred in two facilities near Athens (Malakasa and Ritsona), intensifying concerns for 36,000 people on Aegean islands.
Dutch physician Steven van de Vijver launched a petition urging EU leaders to take in refugees from Greece; over 6,000 European doctors signed.
Greek authorities detected the first coronavirus case in a reception centre at Malakasa and implemented quarantine and isolation measures.
The outbreak in Ritsona was traced to a 19-year-old Cameroonian woman who tested positive after giving birth in an Athens hospital.
NGOs voiced fears over lack of access to testing, medical facilities, and basic services in the camps, and called for evacuation of refugees to other EU countries.
Dutch gynaecologist Sanne van der Kooij said it was a matter of 'when' not 'if' coronavirus strikes the camps, describing poor conditions.
Almost 35,000 European health workers and citizens backed the doctors' petition calling for EU compliance with the 2016 Turkey accord for refugee resettlement.

2-34752-6-2.subevent: Toxic blue-green algae thrive in warm, slow-moving water, and harmful algae usually bloom during warm summer or when water temperatures are warmer than usual.

9-21751-1-3.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday morning in three cities across Israel as police attempted to enforce coronavirus lockdown restrictions in ultra-Orthodox communities.

In Jerusalem's Mea Shearim neighborhood, hundreds of people clashed with police attempting to shut down a yeshiva that had opened illegally; police said officers were surrounded by a crowd shouting insults and throwing trash and debris, with one person arrested and water cannon trucks used to disperse the crowd.

In Ashdod, police were confronted while closing down an ultra-Orthodox elementary school that had opened despite rules; several dozen people tried to force their way into the compound, injuring four officers and damaging the fence, and protesters blocked traffic; four people were arrested.
In Bnei Brak, several clashes broke out as police tried to shut down schools linked to the Vizhnitz Hasidic dynasty, whose head rabbi had initially ruled that schools should open before backtracking.
Police said in response to the violence that they would continue to enforce virus restrictions in all communities.

The lockdown, in its third week and extended till January 31, has shuttered all nonessential businesses along with the entire education system, but some ultra-Orthodox schools have continued to operate in violation of the rules.

Last week clashes broke out between police and rioters opposed to lockdown restrictions in Bnei Brak after a mob injured a police officer; at least six people were arrested, and the rioters belonged to an extremist faction of the Vizhnitz Hasidic sect.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the Friday attack in Bnei Brak, stating that 'we will act with a heavy hand against lawbreakers, first and foremost against those who raised their hands against our policewomen and policemen.'
Critics have accused Netanyahu of avoiding cracking down on the Haredi public in order not to anger his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners.
Additional reports of lockdown violations among the ultra-Orthodox emerged Saturday, including a mass gathering over the weekend in the Sanz Hasidic sect in Netanya.

On Thursday, Health Minister Yuli Edelstein called for jailing those who broke lockdown rules, and Netanyahu and Edelstein appealed to Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky to influence the community to obey the lockdown.

According to Haaretz, Rabbi Kanievsky gave permission for some ultra-Orthodox schools to reopen this week, but only if it does not spark a confrontation with police, and some schools were hesitant to reopen despite his approval.

The Health Ministry reported a further decline in daily coronavirus infections, with 2,394 new cases confirmed on Saturday after peaking at over 10,100 a week earlier; total infections reached 595,097, deaths 4,361, and 1,228 serious cases.

1-15205-8-t.subevent: Bridgett Floyd, sister of George Floyd, urged protesters to 'be his legacy' and said her brother cannot be a voice today.
Ms Floyd was one of several relatives of black Americans harmed or killed by police to address the event commemorating the 1963 civil rights march.
Speakers demanded racial justice and urged people to vote.
Jacob Blake Sr told the rally that they were holding court on racism in America and the verdict was 'guilty'.
Thousands gathered in Washington DC for the Commitment March: Get Your Knee Off Our Necks, which commemorated the 1963 March on Washington and protested police violence.
The event was organized by civil rights leader Reverend Al Sharpton and Martin Luther King III.
The families of black Americans shot or killed by police spoke at the same site where Martin Luther King Jr delivered his I Have a Dream speech.
Rev Sharpton announced the 2020 march at George Floyd's memorial service in June.
Martin Luther King III said the nation has never seen such a mighty movement and they would complete the work begun in the 1960s.
The event came after protests over Jacob Blake's shooting that left two dead in Kenosha, Wisconsin.
Since George Floyd's death in May, Black Lives Matter marches have swept the US and the globe.
Attendees lined Constitution avenue as early as 7am in anticipation of the march.
Lloyd Miner said he was there to play his role and give the administration a mandate for change.
Rex Ikwueme said they were in a crisis and could not see his people die on film every week.
Artelia Bryant said little has changed since 1963 and called for cops to be arrested, starting with those who killed Breonna Taylor.
Many called for the immediate passage of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.
Patrick Reyes said voter suppression still exists and they were demanding justice.
Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley paid tribute to the activism of black Americans and said they are the manifestation of the movement.
Other presenters included a young activist calling for an end to gun violence, and representatives from unions, gay rights groups, and Hispanic activism groups expressing solidarity.
Democratic vice-presidential nominee Kamala Harris addressed the rally virtually, urging to march on for ancestors and children.
Organizers said the agenda included slavery reparations, defunding police departments, and investment in healthcare, housing, and social services in black communities.

25-4120-1-t.subevent: Ten people have been arrested during a climate change protest in Dover aimed at blockading the port.
Four of them, including men aged in their 80s and 90s, staged a sit in at the Eastern Docks Roundabout.
Extinction Rebellion campaigners are legally occupying part of the A20, off the roundabout, and near the port.
The campaign group said the 'No Food on a Dying Planet' protest centred around the potential for food shortages as climate change develops.
Those arrested, on suspicion of public order offences, remain in custody as inquiries continue.
Kent Police set up a designated area on the westbound A20 for activists to demonstrate, in order to minimise disruption.
Traffic leaving the port is being diverted via the A2, on the opposite side of the Eastern Docks Roundabout.
Some protesters also blockaded part of the A2, by gluing themselves to the road.
According to witnesses, one protester who had glued their hands to the road was taken away in a stretcher.
Ch Supt Andy Pritchard, from Kent Police, said disruption was 'kept to a minimum'.
Live music is expected later as part of the demonstration, while flags and signs adorn seafront railings including slogans like 'Rebel for life' and 'Climate breakdown kills'.
The protest was due to last until 15:00 BST.
The protest came a day after thousands of people across the UK took part in a global climate strike day.

Chris Atkins, from Extinction Rebellion Dover, said that as climate change develops, millions of ordinary Britons will face the real and growing threat of food shortages, hunger and starvation, and that the UK is extremely vulnerable due to its dependency on food imports.
A Port of Dover spokeswoman said it was experiencing intermittent delays due to the protest and was working closely with Kent Police to ensure as minimal disruption as possible.

3-16947-3-t.subevent: CRESCO6, one of Italy's most powerful supercomputers, is made available to public and private scientific research against coronavirus.
The supercomputer is operational at the ENEA Center in Portici, near Naples, and can perform up to 1.4 million billion mathematical operations per second.
ENEA President Federico Testa states that the supercomputer can give a vital contribution in this crucial moment for the country's search for drugs, vaccines, and data processing.

Testa adds that the supercomputer is already available to a team of researchers from the University of Florence, coordinated by Professor Piero Procacci, working on blocking the replication mechanism of COVID-19.

HPC CRESCO6 is the second most important public computing infrastructure in Italy after Cineca and is playing a key role in testing the effectiveness of compounds under investigation through atomistic simulations on thousands of processors.
In a few days of testing with the team from the University of Florence, at least two compounds with promising characteristics have been identified, one of which is commercially available.

After this first phase of structural refinement of the obtained compounds, HPC CRESCO6 will be used to try to identify the optimal molecular structure for a possible specific antiviral drug for COVID-19.

Since 2018, CRESCO6 has been included in the prestigious TOP500 list of the world's top 500 supercomputers, after doubling its power to 1.4 million billion mathematical operations per second (1.4 PetaFlops).
Its entry at 420th place was announced at the SuperComputing 2018 conference in Dallas.

Fields of application of CRESCO6 include forecasting models on climate change and air pollution, study of new materials for clean energy, simulations for critical infrastructure management, biotechnologies, computational chemistry, fluid dynamics for aerospace, and code development for nuclear fusion.
Researchers from public and private institutions wishing to submit a request to use ENEA's computational resources can write to crescoforcovid19@enea.it.

7-36258-7-2.subevent: Medical equipment, such as a mobile ultrasound vehicle and a mobile X-ray vehicle, were seen at Singapore Expo on Friday, April 10, as preparations were made for the facility to receive its first batch of Covid-19 patients.
Close to 20 people were seen alighting from two minibuses outside the Expo on Friday night.
This first batch of patients are either recovering or have mild symptoms.
Singapore Expo is the Republic's second community isolation facility.
One hall will house patients in recovery while those with a mild case of the coronavirus will be treated in the other.

Since last month, recovering Covid-19 patients have been transferred from the National Centre for Infectious Diseases to private hospitals, as well as Singapore's first community isolation facility, D'Resort NTUC.

0-4654-1-t.subevent: The New York State Department of Health announced new findings in its investigation into vaping-associated pulmonary illnesses.
Health Commissioner Dr. Howard Zucker urged the public to be vigilant about vaping products and to contact a healthcare provider if they develop unusual symptoms.
The Department issued a health advisory in August alerting health care providers of the emerging health threat.
As of September 5, 2019, the Department received 34 reports of severe pulmonary illness among patients aged 15 to 46 who used at least one cannabis-containing vape product before becoming ill.
Laboratory tests showed very high levels of vitamin E acetate in nearly all cannabis-containing samples analyzed.
At least one vitamin E acetate-containing vape product was linked to each patient who submitted a product for testing.
Vitamin E acetate is not an approved additive for New York State Medical Marijuana Program-authorized vape products and was not found in tested nicotine-based products.
Vitamin E acetate became a key focus of the Department's investigation of potential causes of the pulmonary illnesses.
The Wadsworth Center tested both cannabis and nicotine-containing vape products, as well as the purity of New York's approved medical marijuana products.
More than a dozen product samples from patients were tested for THC, nicotine, synthetic cannabinoids, opioids, and pesticides, among other substances.
Many of the tested products were suspected to be counterfeits of recreational cannabis-containing vape products available in other states.
The Department advised against using unregulated vape products and recommended that non-certified patients consider not using any vape products.

0-4857-5-2.subevent: California faces a critical fire danger due to high winds and low humidity.
PG&E preemptively shut off electricity to more than 700,000 customers due to weather conditions.
Ron Blasingame expressed regret about not buying a generator and criticized PG&E for not clearing brush.
Residents waited in long lines to fill their gas tanks before pumps lost electricity and shut down.
Barry Friedman's home improvement store lost power, but he kept it open by flashlight; some products ran out.
Debbie Medina, who relies on a CPAP machine and oxygen generators, expressed concern for people like herself unable to go to community centers.
PG&E stated that putting existing overhead lines in fire threat areas underground could cost up to $110 billion.

1-15310-1-t.subevent: At least 11 migrants from Africa died when their boat sank off Tunisia on Sunday, according to a Tunisian security official.
The migrants were trying to cross the Mediterranean to the Italian island of Lampedusa.
Tunisia's coast guard recovered the bodies of eight women and three children off the coast near Sfax late on Sunday.
Officials said about 30 people had set out on the boat, aiming to reach Italy.
The coast guard is searching for the other missing people.
Last year, about 90 African migrants drowned after their boat capsized en route to Europe from Libya.

1-14979-1-1.subevent: The Nobel Committee in Physics honored three 'masters of light': Charles Kao, Willard S. Boyle, and George E. Smith.
Kao's discoveries led to today's widespread use of fiber optics.
Boyle and Smith invented the charge-coupled device, which captures light in digital cameras.
Boyle and Smith initially wanted to construct novel electronic memory rather than an imaging device.
The committee honored discoveries made in the late 1960s, violating Nobel's criterion that awards should go to achievements 'during the preceding year'.
This isn't the first time a Nobel Prize has been bestowed for a discovery made much earlier than 'the preceding year'.
The time from initial discovery to Nobel acknowledgment has generally increased since 1901.
It took time for the discoveries' 'benefit on mankind' to be realized.
The committee may have wanted to avoid awkward controversies such as the one surrounding the 1938 award.
Enrico Fermi was recognized in 1938 for his 1934 'discovery' of transuranic elements, only to be disproved the following year.
The spirit of Nobel's intention has remained intact as this year's winners made a fundamental impact.
An article advises physicists doing seminal work today to learn patience.

1-14991-2-2.subevent: Researchers have identified two dozen planets outside our solar system that may have conditions more suitable for life than Earth.
Some of these planets orbit stars that may be better than our sun.
A study led by Washington State University scientist Dirk Schulze-Makuch was published in the journal Astrobiology, detailing characteristics of potential 'superhabitable' planets.
The study describes that superhabitable planets may be older, a little larger, slightly warmer, and possibly wetter than Earth.
The researchers argue that life could more easily thrive on planets that orbit more slowly changing stars with longer lifespans than our sun.
The 24 top contenders for superhabitable planets are all more than 100 light years away.
Schulze-Makuch noted that the study could help focus future observation efforts from telescopes like NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope.
Schulze-Makuch, a geobiologist, teamed up with astronomers Rene Heller and Edward Guinan to identify superhabitability criteria and search among the 4,500 known exoplanets.
The researchers selected planet-star systems with probable terrestrial planets orbiting within the host star’s liquid water habitable zone from the Kepler Object of Interest Exoplanet Archive.
The researchers note that the sun has a relatively short lifespan of less than 10 billion years, and many similar stars might run out of fuel before complex life can develop.
The study also looked at systems with K dwarf stars, which have lifespans of 20 billion to 70 billion years, allowing orbiting planets to be older and giving life more time to advance.
The researchers argue that the sweet spot for life is a planet between 5 billion to 8 billion years old.
A planet that is 10% larger than Earth should have more habitable land, and one with about 1.5 times Earth’s mass would retain its interior heating and atmosphere longer.
The authors argue that a little more water and a mean surface temperature about 5 degrees Celsius greater than Earth would be better for life.
Among the 24 top planet candidates, none meet all the criteria for superhabitable planets, but one has four of the critical characteristics.
Schulze-Makuch commented that it's sometimes difficult to convey the principle of superhabitable planets because we think we have the best planet.

6-18762-1-1.subevent: Biomerieux gave its proprietary formula to the Canadian government for free so its national lab can try to manufacture badly-needed test kits.
Canada passed emergency legislation in March giving the government and third parties the right to produce patented goods without consent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada described the arrangement as a temporary license at no cost, allowing manufacture of Biomerieux products for coronavirus testing.
PHAC said its manufacturing was still in development and testing, aiming to alleviate shortages soon.
In early April, Biomerieux's Canadian unit emailed customers saying the move was meant to clear up testing backlogs.
Biomerieux reported a 21.5% increase in sales in the first quarter, partly due to demand for reagents.
The chemicals in short supply are reagents used to extract RNA from patient samples, and major suppliers face soaring demand.
Biomerieux extraction equipment is widely used in Canada, including as the primary system in Ontario and in Quebec.
PHAC said the deal is an interim solution because its facilities are not meant for long-term manufacturing.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing in its fight against the coronavirus.

1-15195-2-1.subevent: Biomerieux gave its proprietary formula to the Canadian government for free so its national lab can try to manufacture test kits.
Canada passed emergency legislation in March that gave the government and third parties the right to produce patented goods without the patent holders’ consent.

0-4491-3-3.subevent: The Obama administration issued sanctions against Maduro’s administration in 2015 on grounds of human rights violations.
On January 23, 2019, opposition leader Juan Guaidó invoked a constitutional right to assume presidential powers and call for new elections.
Numerous nations in Latin America, Europe, and Canada deemed Maduro’s 2018 election victory illegitimate and recognized Guaidó’s legitimacy.
On Monday, the US government imposed fresh sanctions against Venezuela's national oil firm PDVSA, freezing exchanges and blocking imports.
Guaidó asked congress to appoint new board members to PDVSA just before the US issued the sanctions.
The US redirected PDVSA payments to Guaidó; national security adviser John Bolton said sanctions would block $7 billion in PDVSA assets and over $11 billion in lost export proceeds.
David Smolansky, former mayor, said the sanctions are an effective way to pressure Maduro’s government and have not hurt ordinary Venezuelans.
Rafael Uzcátegui, human rights director, said the sanctions will limit imports of food and medicine and worsen the humanitarian crisis.
In 2017, Venezuela's Supreme Court nullified the opposition-led National Assembly, leading to protests and a violent crackdown that left over 160 dead.
The Trump administration imposed new sanctions against Venezuela in 2017 to limit Maduro's ability to sell assets; Maduro accused the US of exacerbating the economic crisis.
By 2018, the US expanded its sanctions list to include First Lady Cilia Flores and Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.
On January 30, thousands marched in Caracas calling for the end of Maduro; the latest sanctions halt all US oil purchases to support Guaidó.

0-4399-3-1.subevent: The FBI and CISA released a bulletin revealing active Russian cyberattacks targeting U.S. government networks, including those involved with the ongoing election.
The bulletin stated that the Russian hacking group Energetic Bear or FireFly is targeting U.S. state, local, territorial, and tribal government networks, as well as aviation networks.
The bulletin noted that while there may be some risk to elections information, the FBI and CISA have no evidence that the integrity of elections data has been compromised.

U.S. officials said that systems in two local government jurisdictions had been accessed, granting attackers admission to some limited voter data, but they were adamant that the attackers were not in a position to affect results.
Chris Krebs said he saw the announcement as more of a broad cybersecurity statement rather than one specifically focused on election security, since the attacker's intentions were not clear.

Krebs said cyber attackers are opportunistic and in this case used vulnerabilities in county government infrastructures to move within a number of offices, leading them to some publicly available voting data.
Krebs said they have no reason to believe the attackers were looking for election infrastructure or election-related information.
The Washington Post reported that the breached counties are in California and Indiana.
Krebs added that it is possible the group has breached more governments that have not been discovered yet.

The announcement came one day after an in-person briefing by Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe and FBI Director Christopher Wray, in which they warned about Russian interference and an Iranian scheme to intimidate voters with spoof emails.

Ratcliffe, Wray, and others warned that influence-mongers could exploit headlines about cyberattacks and potential exploits to make claims about compromised election systems that might not be legitimate.
Wray said election infrastructure remains resilient and urged skepticism of early unverified claims.

The bulletin alluded that the network activity could enable attackers to access sensitive systems, including by printing access badges, and that attackers may seek access for future disruption, to influence U.S. policies, or to delegitimize government entities.
The Treasury Department announced sanctions on a number of Iranian government entities in connection with election interference.

25-3857-2-t.subevent: Wikipedia users in Germany were met with an error message when attempting to visit the site on Friday.
The website fell victim to a massive DDoS attack on Friday evening in Germany and other parts of Europe.
The website reappeared shortly before midnight on Friday.
The website went offline again early Saturday.
Wikipedia tweeted that it was continuing to work on restoring access later Friday evening.
Social media users shared their Wikipedia woes on Twitter using the hashtag #WikipediaDown.

1-16438-6-t.subevent: WFSA is working with its global membership to curate, share and disseminate up-to-date and practical COVID-19 guidance for anaesthesia and perioperative care providers.
WFSA drew attention to the importance of appropriate precautions for anaesthesiologists and released a statement on healthcare provider safety and wellbeing during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Multiple organizations, including APSF, ASA, IARS, and others, published perioperative considerations and resources for COVID-19.
WFSA released an ATOTW module on perioperative management of COVID-19 cases.
The Lancet published a study on mortality and pulmonary complications in surgery patients with perioperative SARS-CoV-2 infection.
SIAARTI and the Prince of Wales Hospital released guidance on airway management for COVID-19 patients.
UCSF released a ventilator management pocket reference.
SOAP, RCOG, and other bodies released interim considerations and guidance for obstetric anaesthesia during COVID-19.
WFSA curated guidance specifically for anesthesia providers in low-resource settings.
Several national anaesthesia societies, including the Indian Society of Anaesthesiologists and the South African Society of Anaesthesiologists, issued COVID-19 advisories and guidelines.
French, Spanish, and Portuguese language resources were compiled by various societies and governments.
WHO and CDC provided general information, training, and learning resources for healthcare workers on COVID-19.

1-14823-1-1.subevent: The UK and EU set out their negotiating mandates for fisheries this week, with the UK publishing its mandate on Thursday.
On Wednesday, Scottish cabinet secretary Fergus Ewing outlined measures to improve inshore fleet operations and emphasized the sector's economic significance.
EU member states including Spain and France secured special status for fisheries in the EU's negotiating mandate.
On Tuesday, EU chief negotiator Michel Barnier placed fisheries in the context of the desired free trade agreement.
The EU proposed to uphold existing reciprocal access conditions, quota shares, and traditional EU fleet activity, with adjustments only by mutual consent.
Barnier called for a long-term management deal with joint control and inspection, and linked market access to the terms on fisheries access.
Both the UK and EU agreed on the urgency to reach a deal by summer to allow time for annual quota negotiations.
The UK has contingency plans to increase patrol boats and aircraft to exclude EU fishers if no agreement is reached.
The UK put fisheries in a separate section of its mandate called 'Other Agreements', aiming to separate catch access from fish trade.
The UK proposed annual fisheries negotiations for catch shares, similar to the model with Norway.
Britain plans to directly negotiate northern North Sea quotas with Norway starting in 2021.
The UK rejected the Common Fisheries Policy's 'relative stability' principle and will instead use 'zonal attachment'.
The UK stated that EU boats fishing in UK waters must comply with UK rules, and proposed a cooperation forum and dispute mechanism.
The UK government recognized the interests of the devolved administrations in the fisheries agreement.

27-33401-5-2.subevent: Pangkogabwilhan II Marsdya TNI Imran Baidirus visited Poso to survey the situation via air as part of Operasi Tinombala 2020 on Tuesday, December 29, 2020.

After a briefing for Operation Sayap Tarsius in Crew Room Skadron Udara 5, Pangkogabwilhan II, accompanied by Pangkoopsau II Makassar Marsda TNI Minggit Tribowo and Asops Kaskogabwilhan II Brigjen TNI Bobby Rinal Makmun, boarded the AI-737 aircraft.
